'''''Physalis longifolia''''', known by the [[common name]]s '''common groundcherry''', '''longleaf groundcherry''',<ref name=usda>{{PLANTS|id=PHLO4|taxon=Physalis longifolia|accessdate=2 October 2015}}</ref> and '''wild tomatillo''',<ref name=kin>{{ cite journal |author1=Kindscher, K. |author2=Long, Q. |author3=Corbett, S. |author4=Bosnak, K. |author5=Loring, H. |author6=Cohen, M. |author7=Timmermann, B. N. | year = 2012 | title = The Ethnobotany and Ethnopharmacology of Wild Tomatillos, ''Physalis longifolia'' Nutt., and Related ''Physalis'' Species: A Review | journal = Economic Botany | volume = 66 | issue = 3 | pages = 298–310 | doi = 10.1007/s12231-012-9210-7 |s2cid=2794110 | url = http://nativeplants.ku.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/09/Physalis-Ethnobotany-paper.pdf }}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the nightshade family, [[Solanaceae]]. It is native to North America, where it is native to eastern Canada, much of the continental United States,<ref name=usda/> and northern Mexico. It has also been noted as an [[introduced species]] in other regions,<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate = 14 January 2018}}</ref> including parts of the United States outside its native range. In some areas, such as [[California]], it is an occasional [[noxious weed]].<ref name=jeps>{{ cite web | url = http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_IJM.pl?tid=38070 | title = ''Physalis longifolia'' | work = The Jepson eFlora | publisher = Jepson Herbarium, University of California | location = Berkeley | year = 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{ cite web | url = http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=6482 | title = ''Physalis longifolia'' | publisher = Calflora | year = 2013 }}</ref>

This species is a perennial herb growing {{convert|20-60|cm|abbr=on}} tall with somewhat oval-shaped leaf blades {{convert|4-7|cm|abbr=on}} long borne on [[petiole (botany)|petioles]]. Flowers occur in the leaf axils. The bell-shaped corolla is up to {{convert|2|cm|abbr=on}} wide and is yellow with purplish markings around the center. The husk covering the [[berry (botany)|berry]] is up to {{convert|3.5|cm|abbr=on}} long with ten veins.<ref name=jeps/>

There are two [[variety (botany)|varieties]]:<ref name=grin/><ref name=itis>[https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=30603 ''Physalis longifolia''.] ITIS.</ref>
*''P. longifolia'' var. ''longifolia''
*''P. longifolia'' var. ''subglabrata'' (syn. ''P. subglabrata'')

==Uses==
The yellow-green fruit is edible. The fresh fruit "tastes like an [[Effervescence|effervescent]], under-ripened strawberry", and the dried berry "tastes like a cross between a [[raisin]] and dried [[cranberry]]."<ref name=kin/> [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native American groups]] used it for food. The [[Puebloan peoples]] called the fruits ''charoka'' and ''shuma charoka'' and ate them fresh or cooked.<ref name=kin/>

The [[Zuni people]] referred to the plant and its relative ''[[Physalis hederifolia]]'' as ''Ke’tsitokia'', and probably used them in similar ways. Women grew it in household gardens. The [[tomato]]-flavored berry was boiled and ground with [[onion]], [[coriander]], and [[Chili pepper|chilis]] to make a dish considered to be a [[delicacy]]. The fruit was also dried and mixed into [[flour]] for [[bread]]. Today the Zuni use the closely related common [[tomatillo]] (''P. philadelphica'') in a [[sauce]] recipe derived from the traditional dishes that used wild species.<ref name=kin/>

The var. ''subglabrata'' has been listed in government compendia of [[Louisiana]] restricted taxa believed to be [[List of psychoactive plants|hallucinogenic]], but this is likely inaccurate.<ref name=kin/>

''P. longifolia'' is easy to grow in trials and produces a flavorful fruit.<ref name=kin/>
